name: Esther Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for joining me, Esther. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the pension credit centre in the city, a big open-plan floor with about two hundred of us. Pension credit is the top-up for older people on low incomes, so I'm on the phone to pensioners and their families, checking savings, rent and income, and deciding claims. I use an AI assistant all day to summarise long call notes and draft letters, and I've set up a few shortcuts the team now borrows.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the older callers, honestly, some of them want to tell you about their late husband before they'll give you their bank details, and I let them. What wears me out is the targets, we're meant to close eleven cases a day, and the system crashes most Tuesdays. My husband Daniel teaches history at the secondary school, so we both come home talked out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the tools are helpful but nobody needs to panic. Online I'd probably share something about how the assistant saves me time on letters. At church I'd say it's just another tool, like the photocopier was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's pretty good. I already get maybe an hour back each day, and I can spend it on the callers who need more time. I use AI to write the letters, so I've got time to listen to a widowed woman talk about her husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and teach the shortcuts to the newer staff. Daniel and I are saving for a house, we've got about five months of costs put by, and I'd keep that going at three hundred a month. I'd probably go for the team leader training scheme next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a secure job, Daniel's job is secure, and we're on track. The targets are annoying but they're not new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned targets. Do they ever put your job at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I usually hit them, partly because of the AI shortcuts. The people who struggle are the ones who won't touch the tools. My friend Ruth on the next desk is always at nine or ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you and Daniel planning in the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house first, ideally near the school so Daniel can walk. Then children, we'd like three. That's the plan, God willing.

I'd tell people at church it's **just another tool**, like the photocopier.
think: The plateau is **good for me**, giving back about an hour a day.
I use that time for **callers who need more**.
do: Teach my **AI shortcuts** to newer staff on the floor.
Keep saving **three hundred a month** for a house with Daniel.
Apply for the **team leader training** scheme next year.
feel: **Calm**, with two secure jobs and savings on track.

fieldNote: She uses AI to **free time** for the human side of the job.
Her plans are **traditional**: house near the school, then three children.
Targets bother her, but her **tool use** keeps her ahead of them.

steps.text: Teach AI shortcuts to newer staff on the pension credit floor
Apply for the team leader training scheme next year
Keep saving three hundred a month for a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say it's a chance to run the government more cheaply and give taxpayers better value. At work I'd say the people who learn the tools will be fine. Online I'd probably write something hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the floor goes from two hundred to maybe a hundred over a few years. Checking savings and income and drafting decisions is exactly what's on that card. I think I'd be one of the hundred, because I'm already the one others ask for help with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join the team that sets up the new system, because that's where the decisions about our jobs get made. I'd train Ruth myself on the shortcuts so she's not left behind. I'd also start a small weekend business helping older people in our church and street with online forms and phones, maybe forty pounds a visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for others. I believe in a leaner state, but it's different when it's Ruth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You believe in a leaner state, but your own floor would shrink. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very well, honestly. I've always said government should be smaller, and now I'm watching it shrink one desk at a time, starting with my friends. I still think it's right in principle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the weekend business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because older people still need someone they trust to sit with them. My nan won't let a stranger near her bank app. A small second income would also mean we're not relying only on the civil service.

I'd probably keep my job because I'm the **go-to person** for tools.

Start a weekend **digital help** service for older neighbours.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly on behalf of colleagues like Ruth.

fieldNote: She openly names the **contradiction** between a smaller state and her friends' jobs.

Her side business draws on **trust and church ties**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this needs calm leadership and real plans, not panic. At church I'd say we'll look after each other, and mean it. Online I'd keep it practical, sharing how people can prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really frightened. My job is all thinking and phone work, and Daniel's teaching is mostly thinking too, so in 2028 both our incomes are in the firing line at once. Being good with AI tools doesn't help much when the AI can do the whole job without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop house hunting straight away and keep the deposit as a cushion. I'd grow the weekend help business fast, because helping frightened older people face to face is something they'll still want from a person for a while. We'd cut out eating out and the summer trip to Daniel's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. For the first time I'd feel like my curiosity about the tools doesn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's the hardest part. We'd probably wait, because I won't have a baby with both of us about to lose our jobs. Daniel would say trust God, and I do, but I'd still wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your nan about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'll still be the one who comes round to sort her phone. She'd tell me to stop worrying and eat something. Nan's lived through worse.

I'd tell church friends we'll **look after each other**.

steps.text: Stop house hunting and keep the deposit as a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we must take seriously, and the government should help people change jobs, not just pay them off. At work I'd be organising lunchtime sessions on what people could do next. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job still goes around 2031, but five years lets me build the help business into something real. I'd also look at Daniel's side, teaching keeps a person in the room longer than my job does. We'd have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register the help business properly, get insurance and a simple website, and aim for ten regular clients by the end of the first year. I'd keep the pension credit job, maybe drop to four days in year three. We'd put a bit into an index fund each month as a hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy and hopeful. Like I said with the two-year one, the problem there is no time. Five years is enough to have something ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house and the baby in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably buy a smaller house, a two-bed instead of three, and have our first child in a couple of years. With five years' warning we'd still have our first baby, just in a smaller house than we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, still, and the older staff on the floor. Some have been there twenty years and never used anything but the case system. I'd try to bring a couple of them into the help business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the country to plan well, and I'd want it used. At work I'd encourage everyone to start something on the side. At church I'd say we should be ready to help families who struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd be thirty-seven and could have built a business properly. My pension credit job goes by 2036, but by then I could be working for myself. A decade is long enough to stop being a civil servant and start being my own boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for five or six years and build the business slowly. Then I'd leave the civil service around 2032 and run it full time, maybe with two staff. We'd buy the three-bed house and start our family on the original plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than afraid. It feels like a decade to prepare properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your business helps people with forms and phones. Won't AI do that too by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, yes. But a lot of older people want a person they trust at the kitchen table, and the hands-on part, like sorting the phone in their hand, lasts until robots arrive around 2039. I'd shift the business towards visits and company, not just forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep using AI in the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, every day, for bookings and invoices. I'd use it for the back office and keep the visits human.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Daniel and I would both be exposed at once. What would help is easy, fast support for people starting small businesses, and keeping in-person help for pensioners. Old people trusted the pension office because a real voice answered, and that trust shouldn't be thrown away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. A lot of people at our church would turn to each other if this happened. I think communities like ours would carry more of the load, whether the government plans for it or not.

headlineQuote: Old people trusted the pension office because a real voice answered, and that trust shouldn't be thrown away.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old pension credit caseworker** at a large city processing centre.
She uses **AI tools all day** and teaches her shortcuts to others.
She's married to Daniel, a teacher, and holds **traditional, small-state** views and a strong faith.
She's calm in milder pictures but **alarmed** at two years, with both incomes exposed.
Her plan is a **weekend help business** for older people that could become her full-time work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, with **both household incomes** exposed at once.
whatWouldHelp: Fast support for **small businesses** and keeping **in-person help** for pensioners.
